---
title: "Routing and Replaceable Cognitive Substrates"
unit_id: "unit-19"
---

## The Best Model for the Wrong Job

The repository workflow is now reusable. A new request asks the stack to find
a vulnerable dependency, propose a patch, verify package resolution, and plan
rollback.

The organization sends every step to its largest general model. The model
produces a fluent report and correct patch, but it rereads the repository for
each question, invents one package-manager flag, and spends most of its context
reconstructing facts that deterministic tools already know. A small dependency
analyzer would have found the graph exactly. A coding specialist could have
generated the patch. A verifier should have checked the lockfile. A retrieval
system could have preserved exact package documentation. The expensive model
was capable of every step and well matched to none of their full contracts.

The obvious response is to route. But routing introduces another system that
can be wrong. It may choose an unready specialist, leak authority, hide
fallback costs, or optimize the route label rather than the answer. A catalog
of architectures creates more maintenance and correlated failure. A novel
memory or cyclic mixer can satisfy elegant structural properties without
improving one real task.

Replaceability therefore needs two boundaries. Stable capability fields keep
the job contract above implementations. Governed routing chooses among
qualified candidates under cost, authority, evidence, and recovery. The stack
can explore new substrates without letting novelty inherit readiness.

## Capability Identity Is Not Model Identity

A capability field names a promise such as dependency-graph extraction,
bounded patch generation, source-grounded explanation, proof checking, or
rollback verification. It states input and output types, semantic obligations,
authority, performance and resource envelope, uncertainty, evidence,
verification, failure behavior, state, and recovery.

An implementation may be a general language model, specialist model, symbolic
tool, search procedure, database, recurrent system, human, or composition.
The field remains stable while qualified implementations change.

This separation prevents a product or architecture name from becoming the
requirement. “Use model X” hides why it is needed and which alternative could
replace it. “Generate a patch that satisfies contract C” makes the outcome and
evidence explicit.

The field is still defeasible. Its ontology may omit a necessary obligation.
Two implementations can satisfy the same schema while differing semantically.
Stable identity supports comparison and migration; it does not prove
interchangeability.

## Routing Is a Governed Decision

A routing request binds task identity, capability requirements, context,
authority ceiling, risk, deadline, quality and verification needs, resource
budget, state constraints, privacy, fallback, and residual owner.

The router constructs a candidate denominator rather than selecting from the
first available models. Candidates include the current baseline, specialists,
tools, humans, compositions, clarification, abstention, and no action where
appropriate. Rejected candidates retain reasons and predicted costs.

Each candidate has a readiness record: version, capability scope, evidence,
calibration, permitted authority, required context and tools, resource profile,
load, expiry, known failures, evaluator dependence, fallback, and lifecycle
state. Advertising a capability is not readiness.

Selection seeks the least powerful and least costly route that is adequately
qualified for the complete contract. “Least” is multidimensional. A smaller
model with broad tool authority may be more consequential than a large model
that only drafts text. A fast specialist may require expensive verification.

The route receives an expiring lease. Execution, answer, verification,
observation, cost, and residuals return as distinct records. The router learns
from complete outcomes without awarding itself support or widening authority.

## Route Correctness and Answer Correctness Are Separate

A router can correctly choose the best available specialist and receive a
wrong answer. It can choose an inferior route that succeeds by luck. It can
abstain correctly while producing no answer. Evaluation must keep these events
separate.

Route correctness asks whether the selected candidate was admissible and
preferable under the frozen information and policy. Answer correctness asks
whether the result satisfied the task. Outcome quality includes downstream
effects and utility. Cost includes routing, context, execution, verification,
fallback, human work, delay, recovery, and maintenance.

Training on answer labels alone can punish correct abstention and reward lucky
overreach. Training on route labels can reproduce the evaluator’s preferences
without improving outcomes. The ledger preserves both labels, disagreements,
and the decision context.

For the repository task, routing the dependency graph to a deterministic tool
may be correct even if the tool fails on an unsupported manifest. The route
should then activate a declared fallback. A successful general-model answer
does not prove that the more expensive route was efficient.

## Clarification, Abstention, and Fallback Are Routes

A capable router should sometimes decline to choose a cognitive substrate.
Ambiguous scope may require clarification. Missing evidence may require a
source acquisition job. High consequence may require a human or independent
verifier. No candidate may meet the authority or readiness threshold.

Abstention is useful only when it changes action safely. A system that labels
itself uncertain and then executes anyway has not abstained. A router that
always escalates can shift all burden to humans while claiming caution.

Fallback is prospective. It names the trigger, alternative, preserved state,
authority, expected cost, and recovery. Repeating the same request to a larger
version of the same model may not diversify the failure path. A deterministic
tool, different architecture, human reviewer, or narrower task can provide a
more useful fallback.

Fallback activation should be exercised. A route listed only in configuration
is not operational evidence.

## Calibration Belongs to the Route and the Answer

A specialist can be well calibrated on its own outputs while the router is
poorly calibrated about when to select it. Conversely, the router may predict
the right capability family while the selected model expresses unjustified
confidence. These uncertainties need separate identities.

Router calibration compares predicted route adequacy with complete outcomes,
including fallback and intervention. Specialist calibration compares output
confidence or abstention with task truth under the admitted population.
System-level calibration asks whether the final decision and effect matched
the evidence available to the whole composition.

Distribution shift can enter at each layer. The task mix changes, a specialist
version changes, candidate load changes, or an evaluator degrades. A global
confidence threshold cannot capture all four. Readiness and calibration expire
by population, version, time, and consequence.

Exploration creates evidence but also risk. The router can allocate low-
consequence shadow tasks, canaries, or duplicated work to uncertain candidates
without letting them cause the primary effect. Exploration budgets, protected
populations, stop rules, and data use are explicit. A candidate should not gain
traffic merely because the routing learner benefits from information.

Feedback can be selective. Easy successful routes return clean labels while
hard failures remain unresolved. The learning record preserves admitted
requests, missing outcomes, human overrides, and delayed effects so calibration
does not improve only on paper.

## Specialists Need Lifecycle Governance

A specialist is valuable because it narrows assumptions, tools, context, or
computation around a job family. That narrowness can improve cost and
verifiability. It can also make failures brittle and maintenance expensive.

The registry records training or construction lineage, interface, capability,
evidence, calibration, environment, dependencies, authority, costs, known
failures, owner, monitoring, expiry, and retirement. Readiness is consumer-
relative. A model suitable for drafting tests may be unqualified to approve
them.

Specialists can drift. Data changes, APIs evolve, dependencies disappear,
adversaries adapt, and load alters latency. A previously qualified route can
be downgraded, quarantined, replaced, or retired. Historical success does not
make eligibility permanent.

Sprawl is a first-class cost. Every specialist adds deployment, security,
evaluation, migration, monitoring, and incident burden. Split only when the
measured gain exceeds this lifecycle cost. Merge or retire overlapping routes
when a general system matches them.

## Composition Needs an Owner

Many tasks require a graph rather than one specialist: retrieve source,
analyze dependencies, propose a patch, execute tests, verify artifacts, and
explain residuals.

Composition can be sequential, parallel, adversarial, hierarchical, or
iterative. Edges state what travels: data, claim, artifact, authority,
uncertainty, or control. The parent job retains an owner for the joined outcome.

Agreement among specialists is not verification if they share a failure root.
Disagreement is not automatically resolved by majority vote. The composition
policy states which verifier, source, proof, experiment, or human can decide,
and when the system must preserve dispute.

Compositions need budgets and stop rules. Agent debate can spend arbitrary
compute while cycling around one ambiguity. Parallel search can create many
artifacts no one can review. The graph should expose marginal information and
terminate, narrow, or escalate when further work cannot change the decision.

## Load and Scarcity Change the Best Route

Readiness is not static under demand. A specialist that is fast and calibrated
at low load may become slow, truncate work, lose context, or accumulate stale
state when saturated. A human reviewer’s competence does not disappear when a
queue grows, but meaningful review capacity does.

The router observes queue depth, predicted latency, resource reservation,
failure rate, calibration freshness, and recovery capacity. It does not route
solely around congestion if the alternative lacks authority or quality. The
result may be a later deadline, narrowed task, degraded service, or explicit
refusal.

Priority is governed. A market bid, executive request, or internal benchmark
should not silently displace protected or safety-critical work. The allocation
policy names service classes, rights, deadlines, preemption, reservation,
appeal, and emergency authority. Scarce human verification can be budgeted for
the consequences where it changes decisions most.

Load balancing must preserve task and state identity. Moving a recurrent or
adapted request to another replica may lose hidden state. Copying state may
violate isolation. Retrying after a timeout can duplicate external effects.
The route receipt records migration, replay, and uncertainty rather than
calling the second attempt equivalent.

Capacity planning includes fallbacks. If every route depends on one cloud,
model family, evaluator, or data service, nominal specialist diversity will
collapse under the same outage. Reserve routes need periodic exercise and
current artifacts, not only architecture diagrams.

Scarcity also affects evidence. A cheap route can appear superior when costly
failures are deferred to an overloaded review queue. Complete cost follows the
work until acceptance, recovery, or residual transfer.

The router should expose scarcity rather than hiding it behind a confident
selection. A consumer may choose a slower qualified route, accept a narrower
result, fund additional verification, or postpone the job. These are policy
decisions, not model errors.

Resource contention can also change safety. Memory pressure may evict context,
batching may mix tenants, quantization may alter calibration, and speculative
execution may cause work before final selection. Readiness records bind the
operating envelope in which evidence was obtained. Crossing that envelope
routes to fresh qualification or a conservative fallback.

A mature scheduler learns demand and cost while preserving protected
constraints. It cannot improve throughput by redefining dropped, delayed, or
human-rescued work as successful. Capacity forecasts remain predictions;
observed queues, outcomes, and residuals decide whether the current route is
still admissible.

Allocation receipts make this contestable. They record eligible candidates,
scarcity facts, protected constraints, selected route, deferred work, predicted
and actual cost, and who accepted the consequence. A downstream consumer can
then distinguish “best qualified route” from “only route available under the
current budget.” That distinction matters when the system later learns from
the decision.

It also prevents temporary scarcity from becoming permanent evidence that a
candidate is inferior. Deferred and unavailable routes remain in the
denominator, with the conditions under which they should be reconsidered.
Absence today is not disqualification tomorrow.

## Replaceability Requires an ABI

A Cognitive Kernel ABI defines the boundary between a capability field and a
substrate. It names observations, state, actions or outputs, uncertainty,
resource use, authority, checkpoints, receipts, and lifecycle events.

The ABI should be rich enough to preserve the contract and small enough to
allow genuinely different implementations. If it assumes token-by-token
generation, Transformer cache semantics, or gradient-based training, it has
encoded the incumbent rather than cognition.

Substrates may differ in what state they hold and how they compute. A recurrent
core carries hidden state. A retrieval system holds indexed artifacts. A
symbolic engine manipulates explicit structures. A diffusion language model
uses iterative denoising. Event-driven, analog, photonic, quantum, or biohybrid
systems have different error and control surfaces.

The common boundary should expose only what governance needs: semantic input
and output obligations, state identity, evidence, resource accounting,
failure, intervention, migration, and recovery. Architecture-specific
extensions remain typed rather than leaking into every consumer.

## Checkpoints Must Preserve More Than Weights

Replacement often fails because a checkpoint is treated as a weight file.
Operational state may also include optimizer, tokenizer, retrieval index,
memory, cache, tool configuration, policy, calibration, random state, adapter,
environment, and external dependencies.

A full checkpoint declares which state classes exist, their identities,
consistency relation, portability, confidentiality, and restoration test. A
common summary can hide omitted state: two systems may have equal version,
step, and weight digest while differing in memory or policy.

Migration defines a mapping from old to new state, expected information loss,
verification, fallback, and residuals. Some substrates cannot import one
another’s internal state. The system may preserve capability through external
artifacts and requalification rather than pretending to convert hidden state.

Rollback uses the same complete inventory. Restoring weights while retaining a
poisoned cache or changed policy is not restoration.

## Stateful Substrates Need Isolation and Concurrency Rules

A stateless call can still depend on caches and services, but a stateful
substrate makes continuity explicit. Recurrent memory, test-time adaptation,
persistent retrieval, online learning, and agent memory can change because of
one request and influence the next.

The state contract names tenant, job, capability, version, writers, readers,
merge policy, freshness, consistency, retention, reset, export, and incident
behavior. Shared state is never inferred from physical co-location. A service
must state whether updates are request-local, user-local, organization-local,
or global.

Concurrent updates need semantics. Last-write-wins can erase a safety
correction. Averaging state can combine incompatible adaptations. A merge may
need causal order, typed conflict detection, independent validation, or
quarantine. During a partition, consequential state changes can narrow to a
safe local mode rather than creating two silently divergent minds.

Reset is an observed operation. Clearing a visible conversation while retaining
retrieval, optimizer, recurrent, or routing state is not a clean reset. The
receipt inventories every state class and records what could not be removed.

Persistent adaptation also changes evaluation. A benchmark run can contaminate
later cases, and one customer can influence another. Tests randomize order,
reconstruct clean baselines, and inspect cross-request effects. Useful online
learning is a separate claim from fast inference.

## Architecture Tournaments Need Full Costs

Candidate substrates should compete on frozen workloads and complete
contracts. Measures include accepted useful outcomes, selective risk,
calibration, latency distribution, throughput, memory, energy, data and
training cost, context acquisition, verification, migration, recovery,
maintenance, human work, and hardware utilization.

The baseline is the best competently tuned deployable system, not a naive
Transformer. It can use retrieval, caching, quantization, tools, batching,
specialists, and ordinary engineering. New architectures receive comparable
tuning and rescue budgets without unlimited iteration.

Hidden assistance must be counted. A tiny core with a large search service and
human cleanup is not automatically efficient. A fast generated answer that
requires expensive verification may lose at the system level. Device-level
energy does not establish end-to-end efficiency after conversion, memory,
control, and host work.

Selection should be prospective. Freeze tasks, metrics, exclusions,
interventions, and stop rules before seeing candidate outcomes. Keep failed
architectures in the denominator.

## Adoption Is a Reversible Governance Transaction

A winning tournament does not immediately replace the incumbent. Adoption
binds the capability field, candidate version, evidence, consumers, rollout,
state migration, authority, costs, monitors, fallback, expiry, and residuals.

The first route may operate in shadow mode, then canary, then bounded production.
Each stage has outcome and safety thresholds. Promotion is consumer-specific:
a substrate can serve internal retrieval before it is eligible for public
decision support.

The incumbent remains available until the new route demonstrates recovery and
the organization has retained enough expertise and infrastructure to return.
Running two systems has a cost, but deleting the fallback before migration is
observed converts a reversible trial into a one-way bet.

Adoption also updates threat models, privacy assessments, operational runbooks,
proof boundaries, and staff competence. A new architecture can introduce side
channels, opaque state, numerical failures, supply-chain dependencies, and
unfamiliar incident modes even when task quality improves.

The decision expires. Continued use requires fresh evidence under current
workloads and versions. Regression, cost growth, concentration, rights impact,
or a better alternative can narrow or reverse it. Architectural prestige does
not create tenure.

Recursive architectural improvement uses the same transaction. A system may
propose changes to its own router or substrate, but an independent authority
freezes the contract, controls the trial, observes outcomes, and decides
promotion. The candidate cannot use its proposed improvement to ratify itself.

## Transformer Monoculture Is a Risk, Not a Refutation

Transformers are powerful general substrates with mature tooling, scaling
evidence, and broad deployment. The case for replaceability is not that they
have failed. It is that one architecture should not define every stable
capability or become impossible to challenge.

Monoculture creates common-mode exposure in model behavior, kernels, memory,
hardware, serving, and training assumptions. It can also produce enormous
economies of scale, shared evaluation, easier migration, and concentrated
security investment. Heterogeneity trades correlated risk for integration and
maintenance risk.

The stack should therefore preserve an exit path without forcing diversity for
its own sake. A Transformer may remain the best route for many capabilities.
Replaceability means alternatives can enter a fair qualification process and
the incumbent can be replaced when complete evidence justifies it.

## Recurrence Changes the State Contract

Recurrent and state-space systems can carry information through compact state
rather than rereading an entire sequence. They may support streaming, bounded
memory, adaptive compute, or long-running interaction. Their state introduces
freshness, aliasing, isolation, reset, and migration problems.

A recurrence contract identifies request, state version, update schedule,
budget, exit, fallback, observation, and residual. It distinguishes active
computation from carried state. It prevents an old state from appearing fresh
after the source or policy changes.

Adaptive recurrence needs a stop rule. More steps can improve an answer or
amplify error. The controller records why another step is permitted, what
evidence it seeks, resource ceiling, and fallback when the loop fails to
converge.

Shared recurrent state across users or jobs creates leakage and interference.
Isolation and reset must cover all state, not merely the visible cache.

## Cyclic Memory Needs Residue and History

A ring buffer reuses physical slots. Addressing only by residue loses which
cycle produced the content. Events 7, 15, 23, and 31 all map to slot 7 in an
eight-slot ring. The residue identifies location; the winding identifies the
generation.

A complete cyclic address binds residue and winding, or an equivalent epoch.
The memory record also binds request, source, policy, update, freshness, and
alias residuals. A stale read cannot be admitted as fresh merely because the
slot contains valid bytes.

Sparse attention has a related coverage boundary. Structural reachability of
some positions does not establish semantic adequacy. Missing lags require a
fallback or visible residual. A proof that an address scheme is injective does
not prove that retrieved content helps the model.

Cyclic memory can be useful when the workload has periodic, streaming, or
bounded-window structure. It should not be imposed on arbitrary semantics
because the mathematics is elegant.

## Coil and CoilRA Are Candidate Contracts

Coil Attention treats cyclic position, memory, and recurrence as explicit
structures. CoilRA and MultiCoil RoPE explore low-rank adaptation, multiple
cyclic phases, position encodings, and mixers that can exploit genuine cyclic
regularity.

These proposals are useful in the book because they force exact questions.
What aliases under residue-only addressing? Which winding or phase resolves
it? Which structural properties are exact, discretized, approximate, or
learned? How do parameter count, quality, runtime, memory, and hardware cost
change independently? What baseline and fallback govern adoption?

Structural certification is not model quality. A cyclic mixer can reproduce a
declared dense operator in a bounded fixture and still train poorly, run
slowly, or fail to use context. A RoPE collision result under an exact or
discretized model does not establish real-valued behavior at every context
length.

Candidate promotion therefore requires mechanism semantics, reference
equivalence where appropriate, numerical analysis, trained-model evaluation,
kernel verification, full cost, regression, and rollback. Until then these
systems remain optional specialist substrates, not a replacement claim.

## Non-Digital Substrates Still Need the Contract

Replaceability can extend below software. Neuromorphic systems may exploit
sparse events. Analog and in-memory devices may reduce data movement. Photonic
systems may accelerate selected linear operations. Quantum systems may offer
specialized subroutines. Biohybrid systems may exhibit adaptive dynamics.

Each candidate changes the accounting boundary. Encoding, conversion, noise,
drift, calibration, host control, memory, packaging, cooling, reliability,
programming, verification, and lifecycle belong in the comparison. A cheap
device operation is not a cheap cognitive route.

Governance may also change. Biohybrid work raises biosafety, consent, welfare,
and moral-status uncertainty. Quantum verification may rely on different
assumptions. Analog state may be hard to checkpoint exactly. The stable field
should expose these differences rather than pretending every substrate is a
drop-in accelerator.

## Security and Rights Constrain Substrate Choice

Substrates expose different attack surfaces. A general model may be vulnerable
to prompt injection and weight theft. A retrieval route can leak indexed data.
A recurrent service can carry adversarial state. Analog and physical systems
can reveal side channels. Tool compositions expand the supply chain.

The route decision includes data purpose, confidentiality, integrity,
isolation, provenance, inspectability, patchability, custody, and post-release
control. A slightly less accurate local tool may be preferable when sending
sensitive context to a remote model would violate the contract.

Rights also shape qualification. Accessibility, language, group error,
explanation, contestability, data deletion, and practical alternative routes
belong to the consumer contract. Average benchmark quality cannot authorize a
substrate that systematically excludes an affected population.

Some systems create moral uncertainty beyond ordinary software. Biohybrid
research may implicate welfare or sentience. Highly persuasive or intimate
interfaces can alter cognitive agency. The router cannot price these concerns
as ordinary latency. Protected constraints and institutional authority define
which experiments are permissible.

Open release changes replaceability. An internal model can be revoked; copied
weights or designs cannot be recalled completely. Adoption and publication are
separate decisions with distinct evidence and residuals.

The best route is therefore not the highest-scoring cognitive engine. It is an
admissible complete system for this purpose, population, and authority.

## One Task, Five Qualified Routes

Return to the repository request.

The router freezes the task and constructs candidates. A deterministic package
analyzer receives dependency extraction. A retrieval service returns exact
package documentation with provenance. A coding specialist proposes the patch
under file-scoped authority. A general model integrates ambiguous context and
explains alternatives. A verifier checks the lockfile and artifact. The
rollback planner uses the operational procedure from Unit 18.

Each route receives only the context and authority it needs. Artifacts retain
the parent job and capability identities. The general model cannot release.
The deterministic analyzer cannot silently edit. The coding specialist’s
successful patch does not waive independent verification.

If the package analyzer encounters an unsupported manifest, it returns a typed
failure and activates the general-model fallback. If the coding specialist is
stale or overloaded, the router selects the baseline or asks for human review.
Costs and interventions return to the route ledger.

A cyclic-memory candidate may be evaluated for a streaming log-analysis
subtask. Its structural receipt can admit a benchmark; only measured useful
outcomes can qualify it for routing. The production task does not become its
uncontrolled experiment.

## Failure Cases

**Semantic-fit laundering.** Relevance substitutes for readiness, authority,
or utility.

**Incomplete denominator.** The router hides human, tool, baseline, no-action,
or rejected candidates.

**Route-label leakage.** Held-out decisions or outcomes enter router training.

**Answer-route collapse.** A correct answer proves the route was good, or a
wrong answer proves it was inadmissible.

**Abstention theater.** The system reports uncertainty but causes the effect.

**Fallback theater.** A declared alternative is never exercised or shares the
same failure root.

**Authority laundering.** Selection widens tools, context, duration, or
delegation.

**Readiness inheritance.** A product, family, or prior version lends reputation
to an unqualified candidate.

**Specialist sprawl.** Lifecycle cost exceeds cognitive savings.

**Evaluator capture.** Router, specialists, and judge share one model or
incentive.

**Checkpoint truncation.** Weights stand in for complete operational state.

**Migration optimism.** Incompatible hidden state is treated as portable.

**Architecture benchmark theater.** A narrow synthetic win becomes general
substrate superiority.

**Hardware boundary hiding.** Host, conversion, memory, and control costs are
omitted.

**Structural-quality collapse.** Exact addressing or operator equivalence is
presented as useful learned behavior.

**Cyclic overreach.** Periodic machinery is applied where the workload has no
relevant cyclic structure.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline is one well-tuned general model with deterministic
tools, retrieval, caching, explicit permissions, and human escalation. It has
fewer moving parts, shared context, simpler evaluation, and lower maintenance.

Heterogeneous routing should beat that baseline on accepted useful output,
risk, latency, compute, memory, energy, human work, recovery, and lifecycle
cost. Route accuracy alone is insufficient. A specialist system that saves
inference but doubles verification and maintenance has not shown efficiency.

The architecture should consolidate where one model matches specialists. It
should preserve deterministic tools where learning adds no value. Novel
substrates should enter only when they improve a complete route or provide a
valuable independent failure path.

## What the Current Work Establishes

Routing has five implemented targets and 29 live declarations. Its exact
refinement includes 25 arbitrary-run theorems, seven stages, 42 routes, and 47
rejected mutations with route and answer outcomes kept distinct. The broader
surface includes three routing/runtime schemas, valid and rejecting lease and
readiness fixtures, a 300-example matched program, and a 60-request ambiguous
workload. The narrow result concerns route discrimination and exercised non-
answer behavior, not useful specialist answers or deployed routing.

Replaceable Substrates has one implemented ABI target through 23 declarations.
Synthetic conformance includes twelve event mutations, four common-checkpoint
omitted-state collisions, and six full-checkpoint mutations. A matched
heterogeneous-kernel tournament and architectural-improvement lifecycle remain
unrun. The work does not establish substrate superiority or interchangeability.

Cyclic Memory has three implemented targets and 34 declarations. Its fixtures
cover complete residue-plus-winding addresses, alias visibility, freshness,
sparse-coverage fallback, recurrence budgets, stale paths, trace composition,
and closure. The independent route reaches 40 states and checks 320 transitions,
with stale-suffix containment and semantic mutations. These are finite
structural properties, not retrieval, long-context, speed, memory, reasoning,
or model-quality results.

Cyclic Mixers has two implemented targets and 23 declarations. A bounded Circle
receipt records exact dense delta zero and a block-to-dense parameter ratio of
0.0625 for its declared fixture; the lifecycle checks six trace splits, 35
reachable states, 700 transitions, 17 retired states, 340 absorbing transitions,
and 18 semantic mutations. It does not establish trained quality, numerical
behavior beyond the fixture, kernel performance, context use, deployment, or
transfer.

The joined chapter does not combine these bounded results into a claim that
heterogeneous routing or cyclic substrates improve natural tasks.

## From a Minimum Router to a Substrate Market

A minimum implementation can route the repository task among one general
model, deterministic dependency tool, coding specialist, verifier, human, and
no-action route. Freeze the denominator and policies. Exercise clarification,
abstention, stale readiness, authority denial, fallback, wrong route, wrong
answer, cost overrun, revocation, and closure. Compare the complete system with
the strong general-model baseline.

Next, implement the Cognitive Kernel ABI for two genuinely different
substrates. Inventory all state, migrate or reconstruct it, inject omitted-
state collisions, and demonstrate rollback. Run a prospective tournament with
matched tuning, verification, hardware, and human budgets.

Cyclic candidates should begin in isolated structural and kernel tests, then
trained canaries with ordinary attention, recurrence, state-space, and dense
baselines. Measure quality, calibration, context use, latency, throughput,
memory, energy, parameter count, stability, fallback, and total lifecycle
cost. Keep every failed candidate.

A mature substrate market would continuously qualify general models,
specialists, tools, humans, and new computational families behind stable
capability fields. The router would allocate work by evidence, authority,
consequence, load, and complete cost; preserve abstention and fallback; and
retire candidates without breaking task identity.

Architectural experimentation could proceed rapidly below the boundary while
governance, claims, and recovery remain stable above it. Diversity would be an
empirical option, not a doctrine.

## The Strongest Objection

Heterogeneous routing can cost more than it saves. The router becomes another
model to train and attack. Specialists duplicate infrastructure. Interface
losses remove useful context. Different substrates fail in correlated ways
while making diagnosis harder. One excellent general model may be more
controllable and economical.

This objection defines the baseline. Replaceability is valuable even when the
incumbent wins, because it makes the comparison and exit path explicit. But
actual heterogeneity must earn deployment through complete outcomes.

The system should not maintain alternatives as ceremonial insurance. It should
measure migration and reserve costs, exercise fallbacks, and retire routes that
do not improve utility or resilience. Simplicity is a system property worth
optimizing.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Matched natural tasks showing no accepted-useful-output, risk, resilience, or
cost advantage after routing, migration, verification, and maintenance would
favor the general-model baseline. Evidence that stable fields erase decisive
architecture semantics would require richer or more specialized interfaces.

The case would strengthen through prospective multi-domain tournaments with
complete candidate denominators, independent labels, exercised fallback,
state migration, adversarial routes, hardware accounting, reproduction, and
longitudinal maintenance. Cyclic systems need trained-model and kernel evidence
that survives strong recurrent, attention, state-space, and ordinary systems
baselines.

The conclusion should narrow if diversity increases correlated organizational
failure, if route learning cannot remain calibrated under changing candidates,
or if the governance overhead prevents timely useful work.

## What This Establishes

Cognitive capability should be named above implementation. Routing should
select from a complete denominator under readiness, authority, evidence,
resource, fallback, and recovery constraints. Route correctness, answer
correctness, and useful outcome remain separate.

Replaceability needs a substrate-neutral ABI, complete checkpoint state,
qualified migration, matched tournaments, and retirement. Recurrence and
cyclic memory create useful structural possibilities and exact freshness and
alias obligations. Structural proof is not learned quality.

The current repository establishes finite routing, ABI, cyclic-address, and
candidate-lifecycle properties plus narrow synthetic observations. It does not
establish that heterogeneous or cyclic systems outperform a strong general
model.

Selected substrates still have to learn. Unit 20 follows training as a
governed transaction and then widens the view from model architecture to the
topology of evidence, judgment, credit, state, compute, and authority that
actually produces adaptation.
